AsSalaamAlaykum everyone,

Thank you for taking the time to join these sessions. For those of you who do not know me, I would like to take a moment to introduce myself. My name is Asif Hussain. I live in New Jersey, in the United States of America. I am a software engineer by profession. As for my religious education, I have been studying religion — religions, in the plural — since 2001, which means it has been about nineteen years now. I have studied several religions in considerable depth: Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, and of course Islam.

When it comes to the Quran, I am a student of Quranic linguistics. I have a deep interest in Arabic etymology and morphology. You will often hear me trace Arabic words back to their roots to explain their meaning — something I find genuinely fascinating for the way roots convey a word's true depth. What drew me into this, above all else, was the جاھلی poetry of the ancient Arabs. The intensity and imagination of those poets truly captured my interest.

As for these sessions, I have been conducting them for over five years. I began them to share what I had learned with young adults within my family and my community. We live in times when Islam carries a very poor reputation, shaped by everything unfolding around us. I found young people reluctant — almost ashamed — to call themselves Muslims. They saw it as a harsh and cruel religion, one that produces terrorists and fanatics. I wanted to do my part in sharing the beauty of Islam as I have come to appreciate it, and I hope and pray that I have accomplished that to some degree over the years — InshaAllah.

We have some elders in this group, and I am truly honored and humbled by their presence. One of my teachers, Javeed Ziaee, has just joined the group — which, to be frank, makes me nervous and a little afraid. But I also draw courage from his presence, and I pray to Allah that I make him proud. I would not be where I am today without his kind and loving guidance, and his immense patience with me during those early, very confused years of mine. Anything good you hear in these sessions comes from the blessings of my teachers. Anything you find wrong is my own shortcoming and weakness.

One thing I want to emphasize before we begin: my real audience is the young adults in this group. They have always been my focus when delivering these sessions, and I will be speaking directly to you throughout. Before structuring the topics, I reached out to some of you to find out what you would like me to speak about. Quite surprisingly, I received essentially the same response from everyone — or at least very similar ones. The question was: why do I need to learn about the Prophet? How does knowing about a man who lived fourteen hundred years ago, among the Bedouin Arabs, help me in this time and age? How is he relevant to my life? We live in different times; we face different problems and challenges. So how does knowing about the Prophet help me? I thought that was a very honest and very good question. I structured these sessions around it, and I broke the topic into five parts.

In today's session, I would like us to take a step back and understand the purpose of religion itself. What is its foundation? What is the underlying emotion that gives birth to structured religion? Why did Allah create us? Understanding this will, I hope, contextualize the conversation about our messenger. Then we will turn to why we need messengers at all — what is the purpose of sending them? After that, I want to speak about the *experience* of Islam. We always speak about the practices of Islam — the prayers, the fasting, the زکوۃ, the حج — but we never really speak about Islam as an experience. I want to shift the conversation there. Once we have built that foundation and developed this context, we will look at the character of our Prophet and ask whether he is relevant to our times. And then I want to close the sessions with a model for success from the Islamic perspective.

I hope and pray that by the end of these sessions, you will see the relevance of Islam and the Prophet in your lives, and that they will be a source of spiritual strength in your day-to-day lives.

So let us get started:
